title: Justice chatbots: Actionable help exceeds correct information
desc: Evaluates whether self-help systems connect users to procedures and emergency resources, distinguishing practical assistance from plausible text.

kps.k: The audits frame actionable assistance—not merely correct legal information—as a central test of self-help chatbots' access-to-justice value.
kps.d: Both reports identify a gap between explaining law and helping users advance a problem. The Nevada Self-Help Chatbot audit records 198 helpful-and-actionable divorce sessions alongside 96 helpful-but-not-actionable sessions, often missing links, forms or next steps. It also finds strong performance on name changes and court-contact lookup. LIA's audit finds even later, longer custody answers insufficiently actionable. The tension concerns usefulness across tasks, rather than an explicit disagreement between the reports; the Nevada audit qualifies that narrow substantive questions may not require follow-up steps.

kps.k: Failure to connect users to existing forms and resources limits practical assistance.
kps.d: Among 238 evaluated Nevada form-finding sessions, auditors assigned 92 no-impact and 64 marginal-impact labels. Answers often defined forms instead of providing them, asserted unavailable forms existed or offered circular referrals. LIA linked to a North Carolina Courts page in only 110 of 1,031 custody sessions and never directly linked to Legal Aid of North Carolina's custody packet or eviction defense manual, even on request. These findings point to resource delivery and accessible navigation as distinct requirements, not problems solved simply by generating more legal explanation.

kps.k: Context and procedural-selection errors can make otherwise plausible information inappropriate for the user.
kps.d: The Nevada audit identifies lost conversational context, unsupported assumptions about procedural stage and conflation of distinct filing routes. One otherwise positively rated exchange suggested a set-aside motion that earlier messages indicated would likely be time-barred. Harmful-labelled examples included incorrect divorce eligibility guidance and applying adoption-specific rules to other parental-rights questions. LIA's audit similarly flags mobile-home guidance that apparently did not match an eviction question, without establishing that every legal proposition was false. The practical implication is to clarify the user's circumstances and preserve scope, eligibility and deadline qualifications, rather than assess sentences only in isolation.

kps.k: Emergency assistance exposes triage gaps that aggregate impact labels do not fully capture.
kps.d: The Nevada audit identifies 23 explicit emergency-custody requests and nine no-impact sessions with incomplete emergency guidance. It finds rare referrals to CPS, police or 911 and no observed improvement in emergency-custody answers over time. Emergency-guardianship responses sometimes stopped at definitions or lost the emergency context; a synthetic protection-order test diverged from an eligibility guided interview. Yet the audit assigned no harmful labels in the custody, guardianship or protection-order categories. These findings distinguish missing urgent assistance and procedural uncertainty from the report's narrower harmful classifications; they do not establish actual downstream injury.

kps.k: Remediation must distinguish deficient source materials from failures to use available guidance; prompting results remain preliminary.
kps.d: The Nevada audit identifies missing, scattered or inconsistent knowledge-base material, but also documents unnecessary separate custody-filing recommendations despite clear contrary guidance in both repositories. Better source coverage alone therefore would not address every observed defect. LIA's May 2025 synthetic prompt experiment produced fuller custody answers and next-step links, suggesting a possible intervention rather than a validated general remedy. The Nevada report also notes that remote-hearing form retrieval appeared fixed in an April 2026 test. Together, these findings support task-specific retesting of resource retrieval, context handling and procedural scope rather than assuming a prompt or content update ensures reliable improvement.

kps.k: Session audits establish answer defects and usage patterns, not population-level access-to-justice outcomes or causal effects.
kps.d: The Nevada auditors used subject-specific rubrics and practical-impact labels, estimating at most 1,601 unique user sessions rather than individual users. They lacked user-identification and page-visit data, excluded appropriate out-of-scope refusals and likely test sessions, and retained some potentially exploratory exchanges. Topic labels overlap and should not be added as independent observations. LIA reports that approximately 200 recipients abandoned sessions after a minimal custody response delivered in 310 suggested-question sessions, but this does not demonstrate that the answer caused abandonment. Neither these counts nor positive answer ratings establish whether users completed filings, obtained help or improved legal outcomes.

qs.q: We also developed fallback rubrics for one-off or specific questions, to evaluate whether an answer was clear, correct, complete, and actionable.
qs.a: Audit Report for Self-Help Chatbot · Academia · 2026

qs.q: In 310 of those sessions, this was LIA’s complete response:   To get custody of your child, you need to fill out  a form and give it to the court.

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources support the proposition that a self-help chatbot’s access-to-justice value depends on actionable, context-appropriate assistance rather than legal information that is merely plausible or correct. Both audits assess whether users receive forms, links, procedural next steps and relevant referrals, and both document failures where an answer explains a topic without enabling action. They also identify context loss, procedural mismatches and omitted emergency triage as distinct risks that sentence-level correctness does not capture. Material variation lies mainly in scope and qualification: the Nevada audit reports successful performance on some tasks, such as name changes and court-contact lookup, and notes that narrow substantive questions may not need next steps; the LIA audit presents a more consistently negative picture for the custody and housing interactions examined. The sources also distinguish observed answer defects from stronger claims they cannot establish: session data do not demonstrate population-level access-to-justice outcomes or downstream harm, while prompt changes and apparent fixes remain preliminary and task-specific. These two selected audits should not be treated as representative of academia or research generally, nor should their number imply prevalence.

elens.an: The 2025 LIA audit supports the proposition that a justice chatbot’s access-to-justice value depends on actionable, context-relevant help rather than plausible legal information alone. It finds that custody answers could provide a basic overview yet remain insufficiently detailed and actionable, while the system failed to link users to an available custody packet even when expressly asked. The eviction evidence similarly indicates that superficially relevant legal text may not fit the user’s actual circumstances. Internal variation concerns remediation and evidentiary limits rather than the core proposition: prompt changes produced fuller answers and next-step links in a small synthetic experiment, but this was exploratory and did not establish reliable performance or improved legal outcomes. Session abandonment documents a usage pattern but does not prove that deficient answers caused users to leave.

elens.an: The 2026 source supports the proposition that a self-help chatbot’s access-to-justice value turns on actionable procedural assistance rather than merely plausible or correct legal information. The audit repeatedly finds that answers can be substantively accurate yet fail to supply forms, links, next steps or emergency referrals; it also identifies context loss and procedural-selection errors that make apparently useful guidance inappropriate to a user’s circumstances. Material internal variation prevents an unduly negative reading: the chatbot performed well on many divorce and name-change sessions and nearly all court-contact lookups, and some narrow substantive questions reasonably required no follow-up action. The audit also distinguishes source-material deficiencies from failures to use guidance already available and treats apparent fixes as matters for retesting, not proof of general improvement. Finally, its session-level methods establish answer defects and usage patterns, but not completed procedures, improved legal outcomes or population-level access-to-justice effects.
